scenario: AITA for calling out professor for making fun of me in class? | Backstory real quick: (20M) I’m a ginger (orange hair, freckles, and I wear glasses as well) and have been made fun of for it for basically my whole life; I’ve had to hear just about every term in the book from firehead, red, carrot top, firecrotch, etc. All of it really pisses me off but I try to keep it to myself b/c god forbid people think I “can’t take a joke”. On several different occasions a professor I had in one of my tech classes this past semester made “jokes” about it. Second week of the year he says after forgetting my name “I’ll remember you, you’re the guy with no soul” and third week “Oh that’s right EverywhereForever, you’re the ginger with no soul”. Most of the class laughed, I was pissed and too embarrassed to say anything. It stopped for awhile after that though. Towards the end of the semester though he did it again, and I straight lost my cool and said “It’s not funny. How would you like it if I called you baldy every day I walked in?” He didn’t say anything, class was quiet and he just continued with his lesson. I left for the bathroom b/c I was embarrassed and just got it together and walked back into class like nothing happened. The next day a kid talks to me outside class and said I was a dick about it and I just shrugged. Far be it from me to think something as arbitrary as my fucking hair color would be beyond juvenile and insulting remarks in college. AITA for the way I had reacted to this? This was mostly younger kids who had just graduated last year I think so I guess it may have influence on how they think but I wouldn’t expect it from a professor.

Do you think going through the same thing every year changes how someone thinks about what they owe others?

It's beautiful that you have such a strong connection to these holidays and the spiritual practices surrounding them. The repetition of these experiences can indeed have a profound impact on one's perspective on forgiveness and relationships. Research suggests that rituals and practices, like the ones you participate in during Lent, can shape our values and behaviors over time. The repetition of these experiences can lead to a process called "habituation," where the initial emotional response to the practice becomes less intense, but the underlying values and behaviors become more ingrained. In your case, the annual cycle of preparation, fasting, and reflection during Lent may lead to a deeper understanding of the importance of forgiveness and compassion in your relationships. As you reflect on how you treat others during this time, you may become more aware of the ways in which your actions affect those around you. This increased self-awareness can lead to a greater sense of empathy and a more intentional approach to building and maintaining relationships. You may find that you're more inclined to: 1. Practice active listening and understanding 2. Apologize and make amends when needed 3. Show kindness and compassion to those around you 4. Seek forgiveness and work towards healing in your own relationships The repetition of these experiences can also help you develop a greater sense of resilience and adaptability. You may learn to navigate challenging emotions and relationships with more ease, and develop a greater sense of patience and understanding. It's also worth noting that the spiritual practices you engage in during Lent can have a cumulative effect, leading to a deeper sense of personal growth and transformation over time. As you continue to reflect on your relationships and behaviors, you may find that you're becoming a more compassionate, empathetic, and forgiving person. How do you think your experiences during Lent and the other holidays have impacted your relationships and personal growth?
